name: Agent-Based and Game Theory Models
title: Agent-Based and Game Theory Models
answer: Agent-based and game theory models in macroeconomic econometrics study economies as populations of interacting decision makers rather than as a single representative agent. Each household, firm, bank or policymaker is modelled with its own rules, information and objectives, and aggregate outcomes such as growth, inflation or unemployment emerge from their interactions. Game theory supplies the strategic layer, covering bargaining, competition, coordination and commitment between agents who anticipate one another. The approach is used for questions where heterogeneity and strategic response matter, including monetary policy transmission, financial contagion, tax design and market microstructure.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Agent-based and game theory models in macroeconomic econometrics study economies as populations of interacting decision makers rather than as a single representative agent. Each household, firm, bank or policymaker is modelled with its own rules, information and objectives, and aggregate outcomes such as growth, inflation or unemployment emerge from their interactions. Game theory supplies the strategic layer, covering bargaining, competition, coordination and commitment between agents who anticipate one another. The approach is used for questions where heterogeneity and strategic response matter, including monetary policy transmission, financial contagion, tax design and market microstructure.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These models run on simulation code rather than on closed-form solutions, typically in Python, Julia, R, MATLAB or purpose-built platforms such as NetLogo and Mesa. A single run may involve thousands to millions of agents, so compute is spent on repeated stochastic runs, sensitivity sweeps and calibration rather than on one large estimation. Data inputs include national accounts, survey microdata, firm-level panels and administrative records, alongside the parameter values drawn from the econometric literature. Reproducibility depends on versioned code, fixed random seeds and stored parameter files, since results are distributions over runs and not single point estimates.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a question and a matching level of aggregation, then specifies agent rules, market clearing, timing and information structure. Researchers calibrate parameters from microdata or estimate them by indirect inference, simulated method of moments or Bayesian methods that compare simulated and observed moments. Validation checks whether the model reproduces stylised facts and out-of-sample behaviour, and robustness checks vary rules, seeds and parameter ranges. Game theoretic components are solved for equilibrium or learned through reinforcement learning, and results are reported as distributions, impulse responses and scenario comparisons rather than as one forecast.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance rests on documented code, data sources, calibration choices and random seeds, because a simulation can be rerun but not always replicated without them. Where models inform policy, central banks and regulators increasingly expect model risk management, independent review and clear statements of assumption and uncertainty. Privacy and licensing constrain the microdata used for calibration, and confidentiality agreements often limit what can be published.Nothing here is legal, financial or investment advice, and readers should consult qualified professionals on their own circumstances.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward hybrid models that combine agent-based simulation with estimated macroeconomic structure, and toward reinforcement learning agents that learn policy rules instead of following fixed ones. Larger compute budgets and better microdata are pushing calibration from a handful of moments toward richer, more granular targets. Expectations are rising for open code, standard benchmarks and shared protocols so that results can be compared across research groups. At the same time, the limits are becoming clearer, since emergent behaviour is hard to validate and policy conclusions remain sensitive to assumptions about learning and belief formation.
